chapter: The Raeburn band: people and touring
title: Ginnie Powell's interference and her singing of Handy's charts
summary: Handy describes how Ginnie Powell pushed Boyd to change personnel and took the singer's job before marrying Boyd.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: Anyway, what about Ginnie? Ginnie was a good

singer, I liked the way she sang. She interfered a great deal with the music of the band, even as far as getting Boyd to let certain people go, to hire other people. She interfered a great deal on the personal level.

Bad reasons; for personal reasons. She didn't like so and so and that was it, she wanted Boyd to get rid of a guy because she didn't like him, and Boyd did it. She knocked a kid out of a job to get the job for herself, before she married Boyd; they were going together and she was singing with Jerry Wald, with the Jerry Wald Orchestra and she left the band to come out to California to live with Boyd. She would come on the bandstand and they would come over to me and ask me if I minded if she would sing, and I did mind but I said no, I didn't mind. She would sing her song and that would be it for that night. Then two nights later would you mind if Ginnie sang two songs.
Who was the singer at that time, Barbara Cade?

Barbara Cox, I think. The girl that David married. She knocked Barbara out of the job and Boyd hired Ginnie. Ginnie was a better singer than Barbara; in terms of singing he made an improvement. I can't argue against that, what I didn't like was the way it was done.
David said that she always had trouble doing your tunes, you always kept her stretched out right to the limit.
I don't recall that. If there were what seemed to be not easy entrances, not easy changes, there were ways of making it easy, which I taught them, and they never had problems with that again.
David still remembers-- which of those tunes I've forgotten--where you come in modulation and he carries a note and then starts it from a third or whatever the trick was--
A half tone above, I think.
He remembers to this day how to get into that tune.

All he had to do was come down a half tone, which is what I was. Or what he could do was take the note that I left there and use it as the entrance note and come down a half tone to the right note on the next beat, which nothing could be easier than that.
